# Day 3: Biological Databases

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to explain why sequence
data is kept in a small number of internationally coordinated databases
rather than one, describe how those databases are organized by level
(DNA, RNA, protein) following the central dogma, distinguish an official
gene/protein name from a database accession number and explain what each
is for, retrieve a specific record and follow its cross-references from a
nucleotide entry to its protein product, and build an effective PubMed
search query using Boolean operators and quotation marks.

## Why coordinated, worldwide databases

Sequencing produces far more data than any single lab — or even any
single country — can curate alone. As of today, UniProtKB's automatically
annotated tier (TrEMBL) alone holds around 149 million protein sequence
entries, growing continuously; GenBank's own raw nucleotide sequence
files run into the hundreds of gigabytes. Keeping a private, local copy
of "the" database quickly becomes impractical — it goes stale the moment
anyone else in the world submits a new sequence.

The field's answer is the **International Nucleotide Sequence Database
Collaboration (INSDC)**: three sister databases — GenBank (NCBI, USA),
the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA, EMBL-EBI, Europe), and DDBJ (Japan)
— that mirror the same underlying data and synchronize daily. A sequence
submitted to any one of the three becomes visible, in the same format,
through all three within a day. This has been INSDC's policy since its
founding: free and unrestricted access, with no limits on reuse,
redistribution, or republication. Since the 1990s, most major journals
have required that new sequence data be deposited in an INSDC database as
a condition of publication — which is exactly why a sequence you look up
today reflects essentially everything published on it.

## The hierarchy of sequence databases: DNA, RNA, protein

Biological databases are organized to mirror the **central dogma**: DNA
is transcribed into RNA, which is translated into protein. Rather than
one database holding everything about a gene, the field keeps separate,
cross-referenced databases at each level:

- **DNA level** — raw genomic sequence and assemblies. GenBank/ENA/DDBJ
  hold submitted sequences directly; RefSeq (a curated subset at NCBI)
  and Ensembl provide annotated, "cleaned up" genome assemblies with gene
  models already marked out.
- **RNA level** — transcripts. mRNA/cDNA sequences, with their own
  accession series (RefSeq's `NM_` prefix, met below), represent what's
  actually expressed from a gene.
- **Protein level** — the translated product. UniProt is the central
  resource here (below), alongside structure databases like PDB (Day 7)
  and domain/family databases like Pfam, which classifies protein
  families using profile Hidden Markov Models — exactly the profile
  methods Day 5 covers in depth.

Working out *which level* you actually need is the single most useful
habit for searching these databases effectively — a theme this whole
session keeps coming back to.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Sequence database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence_database)
- Wikipedia, [RefSeq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RefSeq)

## Nucleotide vs. protein: GenBank/ENA and UniProt

GenBank and ENA store nucleotide sequences close to how they were
submitted — useful as a raw, comprehensive archive, but with annotation
quality that varies by submitter. **UniProt** takes a different, more
curated approach on the protein side, and is worth understanding in some
detail since it's the resource you'll use most in this course.

UniProtKB, UniProt's main knowledgebase, is split into two tiers:

- **Swiss-Prot** — manually reviewed by curators: function, domain
  structure, post-translational modifications, and cross-references are
  checked by a person, and redundancy is minimized (each protein is
  represented once). Currently around **576,000** entries.
- **TrEMBL** — automatically annotated, unreviewed, generated by
  translating nucleotide sequences at scale. Currently around **149
  million** entries — vastly more, but without a human check.

The two were merged into one resource (UniProt) in 2003, but the
Swiss-Prot/TrEMBL split still matters in practice: a Swiss-Prot entry has
been looked at by a curator, a TrEMBL entry has not. A protein's
promotion from TrEMBL to Swiss-Prot is itself a signal that it was worth
that attention.

A third UniProt component, **UniParc**, stores every unique protein
sequence in the world exactly once, regardless of which source database
it came from, under a stable identifier that is never reused — useful
for recognizing when two entries from different databases are secretly
the same sequence.

## Accession numbers vs. official names

Every database entry has a database-specific identifier — its
**accession number**. It is tempting to treat an accession number as
*the* name for a gene or protein, but it isn't: it's only unique *within
that one database*. The same gene has a different accession in GenBank,
in Ensembl, in UniProt, and in DDBJ.

What *is* shared across every database is the **official symbol** — for
human genes, assigned and maintained by the HGNC (HUGO Gene Nomenclature
Committee) specifically so that everyone means the same thing by, say,
"HBB." Start a search from the official symbol, not a half-remembered
accession number from a colleague — the accession only helps once you
already know which record you want.

NCBI's RefSeq accessions go further and encode the *data level* directly
in a two-letter prefix, so you can tell what you're looking at before
even opening the record:

| Prefix | Level | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `NC_` | Genomic (a complete chromosome) | `NC_000011.10` |
| `NM_` | mRNA | `NM_000518.5` |
| `NP_` | Protein | `NP_000509.1` |
| `NR_` | Non-coding RNA | — |
| `XM_`/`XP_` | *Predicted* mRNA/protein (computed, not yet directly confirmed) | — |

The number after the dot is a **version**: the same accession gets a new
version every time its sequence or annotation is revised, so
`NM_000518.5` and a hypothetical `NM_000518.6` refer to the same record
at two points in time. Always cite the full accession *with* its version
— "NM_000518" alone doesn't pin down which revision you mean.

- Wikipedia, [Accession number (bioinformatics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accession_number_(bioinformatics))

## Worked example: following the *HBB* locus from gene to protein

Put the last two sections together on the same beta-globin (*HBB*) locus
this course keeps returning to. Starting from the official symbol `HBB`
and following real, live cross-references:

| Level | Database | Accession | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gene | NCBI Gene | `3043` | The gene record itself: chromosome 11 (11p15.4), aliases, links out to everything below |
| Genomic (DNA) | RefSeq | `NC_000011.10` | The chromosome 11 sequence this gene sits on |
| Transcript (RNA) | RefSeq | `NM_000518.5` | The mRNA — "hemoglobin subunit beta (HBB), mRNA" |
| Protein | RefSeq | `NP_000509.1` | The translated protein; its record explicitly lists `DBSOURCE: NM_000518.5` — the cross-reference back to its own mRNA |
| Protein | UniProt (Swiss-Prot) | `P68871` | `HBB_HUMAN` — the same protein, reviewed and richly annotated on the UniProt side |

Each row is a different database's record for the *same* underlying
biology, linked by explicit cross-references rather than by everyone
agreeing to reuse one accession number — exactly the "why an accession
number alone isn't enough" point from the previous section, made
concrete. The notebook fetches every one of these records live and shows
the actual cross-reference text.

## Retrieving information: know your level, then search

A search at the wrong level buries what you want under noise. Searching
NCBI's or EBI's top-level, everything-at-once search for "hemoglobin
beta" returns hits mixed across genome, gene, transcript, and protein
records simultaneously — comprehensive, but hard to scan. Searching the
same string directly inside a level-specific database (NCBI Gene,
UniProt) instead returns a short, focused list, usually with the record
you actually want at the top.

Three practical ways to reach a record once you know your level:

- **A level-specific web search** (NCBI Gene, UniProt, ENA) — the most
  direct route once you know what you're looking for.
- **Genome browsers** — UCSC Genome Browser and Ensembl present sequence
  graphically, as a function of position along a chromosome: pick an
  organism and genome build, then a gene, and view its DNA, transcript,
  or protein sequence directly from the browser, no special software
  required.
- **Programmatic/command-line access** — NCBI's E-utilities (used via
  Biopython's `Bio.Entrez` in this session's notebook) let you fetch a
  record by accession number directly, script a search across thousands
  of records, or reproduce a search exactly rather than re-clicking
  through a web form.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [Genome browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome_browser), [UCSC Genome Browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCSC_Genome_Browser), and [Ensembl genome database project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensembl_genome_database_project)

## Searching the biomedical literature: PubMed

Raw sequence and structure records are only half the picture — the
biological interpretation of a gene or protein usually lives in the
published literature. **PubMed**, developed by NCBI on top of the NLM's
MEDLINE database (est. 1971), is the standard way to search it: free,
and covering essentially the entire biomedical literature. As of today it
indexes just over **41 million** records; **PubMed Central (PMC)**, the
free-full-text archive layered on top of it, currently holds about **12.6
million** of those — roughly a third, not "most." A DOI link on a PubMed
record doesn't guarantee free access either; when a paper isn't freely
available, checking a preprint server like **bioRxiv** is often the
fastest way to a free copy of essentially the same content.

**Building efficient queries.** A bare search string is usually too
broad. Two tools narrow it down, and both check out exactly against real
PubMed counts fetched live for `hemoglobin` and `malaria`:

| Query | Result count | Relationship |
|---|---|---|
| `hemoglobin` | 287,934 | — |
| `malaria` | 125,280 | — |
| `hemoglobin AND malaria` | 4,445 | both terms present |
| `hemoglobin OR malaria` | 408,769 | 287,934 + 125,280 − 4,445 — exact set-theory inclusion-exclusion |
| `hemoglobin NOT malaria` | 283,489 | 287,934 − 4,445 — exactly "hemoglobin" minus the overlap |

`AND` narrows (only items with both terms survive), `OR` broadens (either
term is enough), and `NOT` excludes. The middle column isn't a
coincidence: `OR` and `NOT` here behave exactly like set union and set
difference, which is a genuinely useful way to predict what a query will
do before running it.

The second tool is **quotation marks**. Typing two words with a space
between them (`hemoglobin beta`) is treated as `hemoglobin AND beta` —
it matches records with both words *anywhere*, in any order, even in
different fields. Wrapping them in quotes (`"hemoglobin beta"`) instead
requires the exact phrase, adjacent and in that order — a much more
precise, and usually much smaller, result set.

`notebooks/day03-databases-in-code.ipynb` reproduces every real record
and every search count on this page with live code rather than
